Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14228954/assets/362ee182f39f9d5cc1e7597f7e836a6ce802b4762a03c347c5701c0830f3d523.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-5t})^{′}}=\frac{-3{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}}{-5{c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}}=\frac{3{c}_{2}}{5{c}_{1}}{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14228954/assets/bff6e7e5f4772441cdc81c809eadc377d3c2c43bd653d0c5c4f7f306adf79a5e.png)

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable node (sink)}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:
